Team discussions recognized that the single most ideal metal for CO -formate reactors would 2 23 be metallic tin, given its well-established selectivity for CO to formate production, low 2 cost, and low sintering temperature (~200 °C), suggesting low manufacturing cost as well. Tin particulate is relatively easy to suspend in a slurry and cast via FTC methods (Figure 12); however, the most significant challenge of this project was to address the sinterability of the tin particles, a technical challenge recognized since 1958 (Smart, R., et al., 1958) and ultimately solved through this project. The formation of surface tin oxides is established to prevent consolidation of the metallic tin; however, given that tin melts at 232 °C, it is not possible to thermally reduce the oxide (SnO ) without melting 2 the underlying metal. The outcome of tin sintered in either a reducing environment or vacuum is shown in Figure 13, where particles do not effectively sinter, thus yielding poor strength and conductivity. 10 cm Figure 13. Evaluation of intermediate reactionary phases at MSU revealed a solution to the 65- year problem, such that the addition of ammonium chloride during the sintering of tin provided an avenue to chemically reduce SnO , thus allowing the metallic tin to sinter. 2 The reaction pathways and Gibbs free energy of the reactions are shown in Equations 1 and 2 below.
